rect.title: This diagram is drawn from ply.yaml, the file describing this codebase's architecture and verification claims. Each box is a component; chips are functions with their declared checks; arrows are permitted calls (solid) and data flows (dashed); red bars are forbidden calls. A box's grey depth is how strongly it promises to be checked — white means something inside promises nothing, deeper grey means stronger checks promised, and the weakest function sets the whole box's shade. Nothing here is green: green is kept for evidence a run has actually earned, which this render never sees, so a picture full of promises should not look like a picture full of results. Hover anything for its meaning.

g.title: ply.yaml — the document this picture is drawn from. Everything you see here was declared in it; nothing was inferred from code. What each box has actually been checked for is what `cargo ply verify` reports, not this drawing. ply: 1 — the format version every rule below is read under; a version this build does not speak is refused, never guessed at

What this document declares. "0 functions promise nothing" counts functions that end up with nothing checked -- whether nobody wrote any checks for them, or the document switched checking off for them on purpose. Running `cargo ply verify` is what turns promises into results; this line never reports results.

component e2e — maps to Rust module ply_e2e Drives the built binary the way a user does, and depends on nothing. A suite that links the library instead stops testing what ships. It had grown exactly that dependency once; the fix was to move the test rather than widen the rule. state VerifyRun — the structure this component holds. The rows below are its fields: each name was found in the code, and each shape read off what that field really is promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

json — one of the things this component holds; the two overlapping outlines mean a structure of your own -- there is more inside it than this row shows. Written in the code as `serde_json::Value`. The name came from the document; the shape and the type came from the code, so this row cannot say something the source does not. The hatching means Ply has no way to make one of these, which is usually why the functions around it come back unchecked.

exit_code — one of the things this component holds; the dashed outline means the value might not be there at all. Written in the code as `Option<i32>`. The name came from the document; the shape and the type came from the code, so this row cannot say something the source does not.

component attrs — maps to Rust module ply_attrs Stands alone. It is a proc-macro crate, compiled for the machine doing the building rather than the machine the program will run on, so a dependency from here into the library would compile perfectly well and would be wrong: the macro would begin depending on the very thing it exists to annotate. promises nothing as a whole — something inside declares no checks, and one unchecked thing sets the level of everything around it (unclaimed) hollow — promises nothing yet: no functions, no nested components. Saying what it holds is not a promise about how it behaves. Nothing to zoom into; a sketch waiting for claims.

component core — maps to Rust module ply_core Everything Ply knows how to do, with no terminal attached. state Envelope — this document asks to show command, root, diagnostics, coverage, and none of them declare a shape of their own, so none is drawn: a bare name carries no shape, and there is no code here to read one from either declares checks up to tested — checked once against the declared examples and generated inputs — the strongest verdict this could earn if every declared check ran and passed; a promise, never a result this box is this shade because `diag.is_absence` is the weakest thing in it: it declares tested — checked once against the declared examples and generated inputs — nothing here is drawn stronger than its weakest part

component kernel — maps to Rust module ply_core::kernel Decides what a pile of results adds up to: the order that ranks one kind of evidence above another, the rule that a parent is never reported as stronger than its weakest part, and the flags that travel upward beside a verdict without being confused for one. state StatusSet — the structure this component holds. No fields chosen to show what must always be true of a StatusSet, whatever has been done to it: `state.len() <= 7`. Ply checks this by making one of these the only way it can — through the type's own constructor — then calling the type's own operations on it and looking again after every one declares checks up to fuzzed — checked against many random inputs — the strongest verdict this could earn if every declared check ran and passed; a promise, never a result this box is this shade because `StatusSet::len` is the weakest thing in it: it declares fuzzed — checked against many random inputs — nothing here is drawn stronger than its weakest part
